title: A Choir for the Hymn
premise: Dominic Dravenmoor, a pest controller who has spent her life keeping her head down in the fading town of Hymn's Rest, is called to clear an infestation at her grandmother's house—only to find that the 'pests' leave fingerprints and the family photographs now show an extra chair that no one owns. She learns the town's founders bound something beneath the chapel to secure their power, a debt renewed each generation by a ritual that was never finished. When the current elders try to sacrifice her grandmother to close the circle cheaply, Dominic must choose between invisibility and justice: she completes the founders' ritual herself, but inverted, unbinding the thing and letting it claim those who profited from it. In the end, Hymn's Rest loses its protectors and gains its first honest reckoning, and Dominic—no longer invisible—keeps the doors counted for whoever comes next.
about_author: Petra Underhill is the pen name of a former small-town archivist who spent years cataloguing church ledgers and property deeds before turning to horror. She writes about the quiet violence of places that remember more than their people do.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Dominic Dravenmoor as she takes a routine pest-control call to her estranged grandmother's house on Vesper Lane. She notices gnawed wood arranged too neatly, like joinery. The beat is wary competence masking loneliness; Dominic treats every job as a way to stay unnoticed.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Dominic finds five-fingered prints in the dust of the attic—too large, too human, ending mid-stride at a sealed wall. POV stays with her; the emotional beat is the first crack in her professional detachment as she realizes this isn't vermin.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Grandmother Ida insists nothing is wrong, but the family photographs now include a plain wooden chair beside every gathering across sixty years. Dominic's POV; the beat is creeping gaslight-dread as Ida's denial curdles into fear she won't name.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Dominic installs her own counters and chalk marks on every door and window of the house. At dawn one mark is smudged from inside. Her POV; the beat is control fraying—the woman who counts things can no longer trust her count.

chapters.title: Hymn's Rest
chapters.summary: Shifting to the town's view through Dominic's errands: the founding families' names still on every plaque, the chapel that predates the county. She interviews old-timer Ruth Ellery, who goes silent at the word 'founders.' Beat: the sense that the whole town is a locked room.

chapters.title: What Ida Buried
chapters.summary: Ida finally speaks: her own mother served as the ritual's 'keeper' and died mid-ceremony in 1968, leaving the binding unfinished. Dominic's POV; the beat is inherited guilt—I've been running from a job my family left half-done.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: In the chapel archive, Dominic finds the founders' ledger listing payments made 'in kind' every nineteen years, signed by the same seven surnames for two centuries. Third person on Dominic; beat: cold clarity—this isn't haunting, it's bookkeeping.

chapters.title: Nineteen Years
chapters.summary: Ruth Ellery confirms the cycle and warns that the payment is due within weeks—and that the elders intend to pay it with a person this time, not livestock. Dominic's POV; beat: dread sharpening into moral stakes.

chapters.title: The Elders
chapters.summary: Dominic attends a town meeting and watches the founding families—led by bank owner Corwin Ashe—smoothly deflect her questions while deciding Ida's house will be 'condemned.' Her POV; beat: fury at power wearing a civic face.

chapters.title: Condemned
chapters.summary: Inspectors red-tag the house; Ida is moved to a 'care facility' that is really the chapel annex. Dominic breaks in at night and finds the extra chair waiting at Ida's empty bedside. Beat: guilt ignites into resolve—staying invisible means abandoning her.

chapters.title: Below the Chapel
chapters.summary: Dominic maps the chapel's foundations and finds the unfinished ritual chamber: a circle of seven chairs, one broken since 1968, and a door scored with fingerprints from the inside. Her POV; beat: awe and terror—the thing has been knocking politely for fifty years.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Notes
chapters.summary: Reading her great-grandmother's journal, Dominic learns the ritual doesn't bind the thing—it feeds it, and the founders built the hunger deliberately to hold over the town. Beat: the horror reframes from monster to mechanism; rage replaces fear.

chapters.title: An Offer
chapters.summary: Corwin Ashe privately offers Dominic money and Ida's freedom if she takes the keeper's role, revealing they know exactly what she's found. Her POV; beat: temptation and contempt—power trying to corrupt the one person who wants nothing.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Dominic publicly refuses at the harvest service; the congregation's warmth turns to a single held breath, and every photograph in the chapel now shows the chair beside the altar. Beat: isolation—she has burned her invisibility and there is no going back.

chapters.title: Taken
chapters.summary: Ida disappears from the annex on the eve of the ceremony; the elders claim she wandered off. Dominic tracks mud and fingerprint trails to the chapel undercroft. Beat: panic crystallizing into purpose; the countdown begins.

chapters.title: Allies Among the Guilty
chapters.summary: Ruth Ellery and two descendants of founder families defect, giving Dominic the full rite and confessing what their grandparents took. Multi-POV chapter; beat: fragile belonging forged from shared complicity—justice needs witnesses.

chapters.title: The Nineteenth Hour
chapters.summary: Dominic descends during the elders' ceremony, finding Ida bound before the seventh chair as the thing presses against the far door. She disrupts the feeding, and the elders' borrowed vitality visibly fails. Beat: climax ignition—chaos, hymn-singing, collapsing candlelight.

chapters.title: The Inverted Rite
chapters.summary: Dominic completes the ritual backward, speaking the ledger's debts aloud name by name and offering the seventh chair not as tribute but as a seat for judgment. The thing enters the circle and turns toward the founders' line. Beat: terrible awe—justice outside the law arrives.

chapters.title: Reckoning
chapters.summary: The entity claims Ashe and the eldest of each founding line, taking them through the door, which seals itself behind them. The surviving elders are left ordinary, mortal, accountable. Beat: catharsis shadowed by cost—Dominic watches, and does not look away.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Days later: Ida recovering, the photographs showing only people again, the town unsettled but breathing. Dominic repairs the broken seventh chair and leaves it standing. Beat: grief and relief braided together; the house feels like hers for the first time.

chapters.title: Keeper No More
chapters.summary: Dominic formally ends the keeper lineage, burning the ledger's blank pages and keeping only the record of debts paid. Ruth asks who will watch the door now. Beat: identity remade—from invisible to responsible; belonging chosen, not inherited.

chapters.title: A Choir for the Hymn
chapters.summary: Final chapter: months on, Dominic still keeps the lights on and the doors counted—not from fear but as a promise. On Vesper Lane, faint and many-voiced, something sings back in harmony rather than hunger. Beat: resolution with an open window—the town listens, and for once, answers.
